Title: Retro Pop, Psych, and Rock Collide on The F16s’ ‘All Dogs Go To Heaven’
Body: It’s their first LP in a decade. That statement by itself might sound very outrageous, but it has been pretty hunky dory for a fan of the four-piece from Chennai since the release of their second full-length “Triggerpunkte” in 2016. They steadily dropped smaller chunks of music in the form of amazing singles and EPs “WKND FRNDS” and “Is It Time to Eat the Rich Yet?”, before taking some time off to work on their third record “All Dogs Go To Heaven”. I feel like The F16s are the kind of band whose sonics keep evolving and changing, but they still maintain a very cohesive atmosphere around them, their music oozes that “them” factor. Teased with the banging single “Mt. Whateverest”, this is a record a lot of people have been waiting for, so let’s get into it. Track one. “Fee Fi Fo Fum”. A sinister-sounding riff which sounds like it would be right at home as the score of a Mexican standoff eases into a slow, laid-back instrumental which has an almost beachy vibe to it. Those dissonant chords that play in the middle of the progressions scratch that itch in my brain, beautiful. It swells into this bittersweet jazzy ballad, almost like a two-for-one song. Title: Rito Riba’s ‘Dilfek’ Pairs 80s Funk and Folk Phrasing with Timeless Romance
Body: Rito Riba’s name reached most people in 2022, when he auditioned for Indian Idol 13 with “Heer Ranjha”, a song he had written himself, and when he did not make the final cut there was enough noise online that a petition went up asking the show to take him back. It never did, and that turned out to matter very little, because the song was released properly that October with Rajat Nagpal producing and found the audience the show had declined to hand him. Everything since has been a result of steady work than a dramatic revival. He has crossed twenty songs, sung for films, recorded with Shreya Ghoshal, and last year released Native Notes , a five-track EP in his own language that turned his writing back towards Pasighat. Dilfek , which came out this October through Play DMF, goes the other way. It runs five songs and fifteen minutes, composed by Riba, produced by Tongs Kichu and written with Saaheal and Siddhant Kaushal, and all of it is about love in one state or another. Title: EXCISE DEPT’s SHOPNOBHUMI Explores the Multitudes of India Through the Lenses of Partition
Body: The style-defying, hard-hitting collective EXCISE DEPT came through with their 2nd LP “SHOPNOBHUMI” in October of 2026. Their first release as new signees of Dialled In Records, this marks an important landmark in their career. There is a lot, LOT more to this record than meets the eye, so let’s get into it. But before that, let’s talk about the website ( excisedept.com ) first. Originally being shared through exclusive emailers which only people who signed up for it received, the website opens up to a dark abyss, with a plethora of rocks all around it. You can scroll through these and click on each of them. Clicking on a rock feels like going into a whole different world, with each having its own music, clippings of letters, and images (the faces are distorted and/or covered with rocks, illustrating the loss of mementos and in a way, history itself). It acts like a forgotten and desperate recollection of memories, which is the theme that this whole record hinges on. There is a lot to unpack here. Title: Aamir’s ‘The Essence of Timing:’ Unpretentious, Warm Indie-Jazz Built on Songwriting Depth
Body: "the essence of timing' is straight off the bat, uncomplicated. One of the highlights of the album is the generous focus each element is offered, given its streamlined use of instruments. It discards unnecessary solos and instrumental breakaways, which he is very capable of. Instead he chooses to rely on the strength of his songwriting. Furthermore this project has been rearing to to see the light of day with some of his numbers being in the works for upwards of half a decade. And while the EP does hint at a possible longer tracklist as the initial plan, it provides a successful glimpse of Aamir's versatile abilities that I imagine will be honed in his debut album. At the heart of this project Aamir is a songwriter. The function defines the form. The songs aren't witchcraft but measured vials of cute potion. I use this term lovingly and not with the seemingly derogatory reputation it has built. Don't come at me. The songs don't break necks or tear open some road to unchartered territory. It is a crystallisation of his innocence that's unbreakable. Aamir is in no rush to prove himself as a sophisticated songwriter, instrumentalist or lyricist and that is the probably the best thing

Title: Albela’s ‘Beetta Waqt Hi Dawai Hai’ Blends Atmospheric Soundscapes With Haunting Delivery
Body: This year, the Indian music scene has kept evolving new sounds, new voices, and more artists willing to take risks with how they say things. Amid all that movement, Albela has been one of the artists quietly doing it his own way. What makes Albela stand out isn't just what he says, but how he makes you see it. He takes the small, overlooked parts of daily life and hands them back with fresh weight, and few artists make listeners feel this seen. His writing is observant , his voice is assured, and his delivery is so magnetic that you stay with him from the first line to the last. That is a big part of why his audience stays so devoted. His latest project, Beetta Waqt Hi Dawai Hai , begins with a title that carries a lot of meaning. Most of us grew up hearing that time heals every wound. Albela borrows that familiar comfort, but the title says something more precise: beetta waqt , time that has already passed, is the only cure. Healing doesn't arrive in the middle of the pain. It shows up in hindsight, as the days go by and the hurt slowly loosens its grip. Albela shares that the album was inspired by the story of a dragonfly. Title: Indrani’s ‘Even If You Beat Me’ EP Blends Raw Pop with House-Party Nostalgia
Body: Even If You Beat Me opens with the line “everything is boring,” and yet it’s anything but. There isn’t a dull second on it. The EP feels like the soundtrack to a house party the listener has been invited to. It was mastered by Grammy-nominated Andrew Garver, produced and mixed by Sidharth Gupta of Green Park and Utkarsh Varma and released through their new independent label, Indimints Records, it explores love, identity, purpose, ennui, and defiance against the backdrop of a move to a new city and the uncertainty of building a career. It also traces falling in love and the tenderness, anger, ache, and decay that can come with it, alongside friendship, yearning, and the extraordinary joy of life. Love Beams is a banger, straight outta America’s 20s pop. Lana Del Rey-esque lyrical lore plays out over a bop beat, and a lush, textured sound unfolds around it. I don’t get existential But still can’t go to bed And I have never been better without The thought of you in my head Not Today addresses the point in a relationship where the same fight keeps repeating. Title: Nyima Vol. 2 Is a Collective Conversation of South Asian Women in Music
Body: During a time when women are raising their voices more actively than ever, there is a distinct, collective warmth that settles over you when you're soaking in a work of art created by women. I don't know quite how to explain it, but it’s a feeling I think every woman has experienced at least once in her life. Be it because of a movie, an art exhibition, or an anthology, it’s just this immediate sense of familiarity and sisterhood that engulfs you from within when you witness it. That exact feeling hit me all over again while listening to a new compilation album featuring independent women artists. Following up on a remarkable debut, Nyima Records (under Femme Music) has returned with Nyima Vol. 2, an 11-track compilation album that, to me, felt like a room full of women sitting together, each taking turns to share a personal story, a lingering worry, or a gentle reflection. That deliberate, intimate feel is no accident as the careful curation behind the record is evident in the selection process. Title: Aryan Katoch’s ‘Chaar Khaane’ EP Delivers Melodic, String-Laden Indie Storytelling
Body: Most heartbreak records want you to take a side, but Chaar Khaane EP , the latest release from Aryan Katoch , only asks you to stay with its protagonist for four songs and watch what longing does to a man. It is short and tightly told, and somewhere around the second song, I stopped listening to a story and started recognizing my own. “Teri Main”, the first song in the EP opens with nothing but an arpeggiated ukulele and a voice, and the voice gives away the mood immediately. It sounds like someone already waiting. The lyrical image at the centre of the opener is lovely: the narrator imagines himself as sand and the person he loves as water, two things that are nothing alone and become a home once they come together. It reminded me of the classic “Mai Rang Sharbaton Ka” and its sweet-water imagery of dissolving into someone else, and Aryan’s version holds its own beside it. The sound of the beach water in the interlude pushes the emotion further, and the restrained orchestration lifts the verses and returns for the final chorus. Title: Hurricane Blends Nostalgia and Explosive Production on the Dynamic :: distortion ::
Body: Hurricane, producer-extraordinaire is back with his next full length LP titled “: : distortion: :”, which marks his third release under Seedhe Maut’s DL91 era. I was a huge fan of both DL91 FM and GORE!, so I was obviously very excited to see what he would come through with for this release. Seeing all the armor visuals and the cryptic posts he was making before it dropped, I could tell that this was going to be a very personal record for him. Little did I know that this would be a masterclass in production too. "pieces/places" comes in strong as an intro, starting with a groovy bassline which is then joined by an electric piano which sounds like it came straight from The Neptunes’ studio. The drum and percussion choices are very interesting, they give it a new-school twist. We go on next to "Ipod Shuffle", which starts off nice and slow, then the drums come in with a complete rhythmic curveball. Definitely caught me off guard, but it goes so hard. Sounds like an early 2000s game soundtrack, and I believe that atmosphere is what Hurricane is trying to recreate, coupled with the sound effects (which he said he uses to portray nostalgia and his childhood). Title: Bulli Bainbridge Blends Retro Pop and Honest Storytelling on Self-Titled Album
Body: Zain Calcuttawala has spent a big chunk of his working life in the parts of the music industry that sit just outside the limelight. He started out as an artist manager and gig programmer at BlueFrog and OML, working with acts like Megadeth, Imogen Heap and T-Pain, and since 2014 he has been producing for artists across the indie scene, including Dot., Tejas, Irfana and Akshath, while also teaching, designing an artist development programme and founding the mental health podcast Marbles Lost & Found . His debut album as Bulli Bainbridge, Seasons , came out in January 2023 and was listed among Rolling Stone’s top ten indie albums of that year, and yet, with all of that behind him, he says he never quite had a body of work that felt like his own. The self-titled record he released this September is his answer to that, a seven-track album drawn from true stories in his life and shaped in the sounds and textures of the 70s and 80s he so loves still.
